lead: Two women who waited on God stand side by side today. Sarai, worn down by waiting, makes a plan of her own, and three people are hurt by it. Mary, who waits and lets God act, sings. Between them the epistle gives the secret of such waiting: “your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3). On the memorial of Our Lady of Lourdes, her song turns our eyes to the lowly and the sick.

set: Ten years have passed in Canaan (16:3), and God's promise of a son to Abram (15:4) has not yet come true. Ancient Near Eastern law collections and contracts know the custom by which a childless wife gave her slave woman to her husband, and the child counted as the wife's. Sarai is doing something her world would have called sensible. The story shows what it costs. Hagar is an Egyptian and a slave, and nobody asks her anything: she is not given one word until the angel finds her in the wilderness.
str: vv. 1–2: Sarai's plan, and Abram listens.
vv. 3–4: Hagar is given to Abram; she conceives and despises her mistress.
v. 6: Abram hands Hagar over; Sarai deals harshly with her; Hagar runs away.
kw: A female slave attached to her mistress. The word is repeated through the chapter, and only the angel will call Hagar by her name.
Sarai's word in v. 5, the same word used for the violence that filled the earth before the flood (Genesis 6:11). She feels this deeply, and yet she goes on to do harm herself.

From ‘ānāh, to afflict, the same verb used of what Egypt will do to Abram's descendants (15:13; Exodus 1:11–12). Here an Egyptian slave suffers it from a Hebrew mistress. Scripture does not hide the sins of its own heroes.
vv: You see that the Lord has prevented me from bearing children
Sarai sees God's hand only as a closed door. So she tries another door. The whole chapter asks what happens when we stop waiting for God and do his work for him.
And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.

Many readers hear an echo of Eden: “you have listened to the voice of your wife” (3:17). In v. 3 she “took” and “gave” to her husband, as in 3:6. The pattern of the first sin returns inside the family of promise.
Your slave-girl is in your power; do to her as you please.
Abram, who believed so greatly in chapter 15, here does nothing to protect the woman who bears his child. The great man of faith is shown failing.
ch: The Catechism says that couples who find they cannot have children suffer greatly (CCC 2374), and it teaches that using a third person to bear a child offends against the unity of marriage (CCC 2376). It also explains that the understanding of marriage's unity developed slowly under the old Law, and that the patriarchs' polygamy was not yet explicitly rejected (CCC 1610). Scripture reports these things without approving them, and it lets us see the sorrow they bring.

set: Mary has gone in haste to Elizabeth, who has called her blessed “who believed” (1:45). This is her answer, the song known by its first Latin word, Magnificat. It is woven from the Old Testament, above all the song of Hannah, another woman God lifted up: “He raises up the poor from the dust” (1 Samuel 2:8). Mary stands as the daughter of Israel in whom the promise to Abraham reaches its goal, and the song ends with his name.
str: vv. 46–49: what God has done for Mary.
v. 50: his mercy from generation to generation.
vv. 51–53: the great reversal: the proud and the lowly, the rich and the hungry.
vv. 54–55: the promise to Abraham kept.
kw: To make great, to declare great. Mary adds nothing to God; she lets his greatness be seen. Her whole self, “my soul” and “my spirit”, does this.
Not the inner virtue only, but a low condition: being small, of no account. Hannah asks God to look on her “misery” (1 Samuel 1:11), and the Greek Bible uses this same word there.
Often taken as the Greek for the Hebrew ḥesed, God's faithful covenant love. It appears twice in the song (vv. 50, 54).
vv: for he has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant. Surely, from now on all generations will call me blessed
A village girl from Nazareth says that every age will call her blessed, and every age has. The reason is in the first half of the verse: God looked at her.
He has brought down the powerful from their thrones, and lifted up the lowly

The verbs are in the past tense, although Mary sings before any of this is visible. She speaks as the prophets do, seeing God's future as already done. Mary's joy is not a retreat from the world's suffering.
according to the promise he made to our ancestors, to Abraham and to his descendants forever
The promise of the stars in Genesis 15 is remembered here. God has not forgotten it. What Sarai could not bring about by her plan, God brings about in his own way.
ch: The Catechism calls the Magnificat the song both of the Mother of God and of the Church, a song of thanksgiving for the fullness of graces poured out in the economy of salvation (CCC 2619). It quotes “all generations will call me blessed” as the ground of the Church's devotion to Mary (CCC 971). St Ambrose wrote: let the soul of Mary be in each of us to magnify the Lord, and the spirit of Mary to rejoice in God (in substance, on Luke).

rite: On 11 February 1858, at the grotto of Massabielle near Lourdes, the Blessed Virgin appeared to Bernadette Soubirous, a poor girl of fourteen, the first of eighteen apparitions. On 25 March she named herself: “I am the Immaculate Conception.” St John Paul II made this day the World Day of the Sick. The Magnificat fits it exactly: the Lord chose a lowly child as his witness, and the sick, who are often pushed to the edge, are given the first place. In this first week of the Great Fast, let us remember the sick of our own parish and visit one of them.
study: Sarai could not wait and made a plan of her own. Where am I doing God's work for him, and who is paying for it?
Mary sings before anything is visible. What has God already done in my life that I can thank him for today, even if much is still unfinished?
